rv.q: More than a little fun, as it turns out, as Giulia is a grand, gothic, and often incoherent but deeply felt passion project from someone new to the world of writing musical theater who, in her first outing in the form, has thrown together a brew of every trope that interests her at once.
Nettles overly relies on cadences bound to remind audience members of “Hamilton” (and “Suffs,” to a lesser extent), but she has also written evocative, instantly impactful melodies.
With Zimmerman’s expert direction, Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo has that magical stage chemistry that fuses disparate elements into a work of undeniable beauty.
It is a remarkable and resonant theatrical experience.
The confidence and ebullience of the production’s excellent 13-member ensemble succeed in making Giulia certainly play like a hit show.
Gorgeous sets, eye-catching costuming, and a strong cast singing catchy songs make Giulia the queen of the hour.
There is much to love, and much to cheer for, in Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo, down to its fantastic “encore” song.

Jennifer Nettles’ lavishly produced new musical at the Arts Center is a curious contradiction: a feast for the eyes and forcefully performed, but hampered by blunt characterizations, an uneven score and an earnest tone that makes the evening heavier than it ought to be.
Giulia sometimes gives the sense of trying very hard to be something that it is not—Hamilton, for example—while not yet embracing the pleasurably rageful id at its core.
Unfortunately, while there are several entertaining elements, Giulia doesn’t quite come together for a satisfying whole.
Giulia lays out several promising ingredients which director Mary Zimmerman doesn’t properly batch into a satisfying elixir, failing mainly as a cohesive narrative about Tofana’s life.
But the production at PAC NYC, directed by Mary Zimmerman, appeals far more for its look and its sound than for its language and its story.
Right now, Giulia is an intriguing cocktail, but it could stand to be a little pickier about what goes into the potion.
But the show's clanky structure and single-minded insistence on uplift, whitewashing her heroine's crimes, make it a bit of a bore.
There are kernels of good songs in Nettles’ score, but every catchy tune gets swamped by Cian McCarthy’s orchestrations that bring a “Les Miz”-overstatement to each of them.

Thanks to director Mary Zimmerman, scenic designer Daniel Ostling, and lighting designer T.J. Gerckens, there is remarkable artistry on display at PAC NYC, where the thrilling new musical Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo opened tonight.
With tinkering to the plot and design, and overall narrative tightening, Giulia is poised to join the ranks of truly great new stage musicals.
Jennifer Nettles' songwriting instincts are sharper than the historical drama built to house them, leaving Giulia a showcase for a talent still finding its true subject.
The brilliantly-named musical Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo is written by award-winner Jennifer Nettles – the story, based on some person in actual history, is completely irrelevant.

Ultimately, it reveals itself to be a vanity project, courtesy of Jennifer Nettles—a Grammy‑winning country‑pop singer who began acting late in her career, starring in deep‑in‑the‑run musicals like Chicago and Waitress.
For all its merits, though, Giulia is ultimately a letdown.

cn.t: Critics find Jennifer Nettles' ambitious musical visually stunning with catchy songs, but hampered by an overly earnest tone and uneven book. The production dazzles technically while struggling to balance its dark subject matter with entertainment.

vr.q: I can't say that this is the tidiest or most thoughtfully rendered story, but actually my biggest gripe with the show was the lyrics more than the book or the music.
the potency you'd expect from a musical about a 'poison queen' falls a little flat
the show has a ton of potential... but as is, it just feels like a big missed opportunity
